title: Operational readiness, maintenance and inspections of life-saving appliances
what: All life-saving appliances must be in working order and ready for immediate use at all times before the ship leaves port and at all times during the voyage.
evidence: Maintenance records, signed checklists, log book
detailBullets: Maintenance is carried out in accordance with onboard maintenance instructions or a planned maintenance programme.
The instructions include checklists, servicing schedules, a troubleshooting guide and a record of inspections and maintenance.
Spare parts and repair equipment are provided for the appliances subject to wear or consumption.
Weekly, monthly and annual regimes all flow from this regulation — see the linked cards.
Falls used in launching are turned end-for-end and renewed as required by this regulation and the maker's instructions.

title: Weekly inspection and tests of survival craft and alarms
what: Every week the survival craft, rescue boats and launching appliances are visually inspected, the lifeboat and rescue boat engines are run, and the general emergency alarm is tested.
detailBullets: Visual inspection of all survival craft, rescue boats and launching appliances to confirm readiness for use.
Lifeboat and rescue boat engines run for the period stated in the instructions.
General emergency alarm system tested.
The result of each weekly item is recorded in the log book.
A defect found on the weekly round is raised as a deficiency the same day, not carried forward to the monthly inspection.

title: Monthly inspection of life-saving appliances and movement of lifeboats
what: Every month all life-saving appliances are inspected using the checklist in the onboard maintenance instructions, and each lifeboat is moved from its stowed position.
detailBullets: The inspection covers the lifeboat equipment inventory as well as the appliances themselves.
Each lifeboat is moved from its stowed position, without any person on board, so far as is necessary to demonstrate satisfactory operation.
Where weather conditions prevent the movement, the reason is recorded in the log book.
The completed checklist is retained on board as the evidence.
The report of the inspection is entered in the log book.

title: Servicing of inflatable liferafts, lifejackets and hydrostatic release units
what: Inflatable liferafts, inflatable lifejackets and marine evacuation systems are serviced at an approved servicing station, and hydrostatic release units are serviced or replaced, at the intervals set by this regulation.
howOften: 12 months (HSSC ±3 months); HRUs 24 months or per maker
detailBullets: Servicing is at intervals not exceeding 12 months, with the harmonised survey window of ±3 months.
In special cases the Administration may extend the interval — Liberia and Panama provide for an extension to 17 months.
Servicing stations are approved under Resolution A.761(18).
Disposable hydrostatic release units are replaced at 24-month intervals; serviceable units go to an approved station.
Keep the servicing certificate on board — its absence is a finding even when the raft is physically in date.

flagNotes.LIB: Liberia SAF-001 provides for a liferaft servicing extension to 17 months by dispensation.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 provides for extensions up to 17 months for certain inflatable equipment with Administration authorisation.

title: Falls used in launching — end-for-end and renewal
what: Falls used in launching are turned end-for-end and renewed at the intervals required by this regulation and by the manufacturer's instructions.
howOften: Per SOLAS III/20 and the maker
evidence: Log book entry, signed, wire certificate, Service report
detailBullets: Read the intervals from the current text of SOLAS III/20 and from the maker's manual — this app deliberately does not assert a figure.
Record the date the wire was fitted, the date it was turned end-for-end and the date it was renewed, with the wire certificate number.
Falls are also examined at the annual thorough examination of the launching appliance.
Some Administrations do not accept bulldog grips on load-bearing wire terminations.
Broken wires at the sheave contact zones are the usual reason for early renewal.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: bulldog grips are not accepted on load-bearing wire terminations.

title: Records of inspections, maintenance and servicing
what: Records of the inspections, maintenance and servicing required by this regulation are kept on board and are available to the surveyor and to the port State control officer.
evidence: Maintenance records, Signed checklist, Service report
detailBullets: Weekly and monthly results are entered in the log book; the monthly checklist is retained.
Service reports and certificates from providers are filed with the equipment record.
A record that cannot be produced at the survey is treated as work not done.
Panama expressly allows the records to be paper or computer-based on board — see the FLAG section.
DeckWatch is a record-keeping aid; it does not replace the vessel's own approved records.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 allows records to be kept on paper or computer-based on board.
flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: reports countersigned by the Company representative or the Master.

title: Emergency training and drills
what: Every crew member takes part in an abandon-ship drill and a fire drill at the intervals required by this regulation, and the drills are recorded.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, drill record
detailBullets: Read the drill intervals and the lifeboat launching requirements from the current text of SOLAS III/19.
Each drill is recorded; if a full drill is not held, an entry states the circumstances and the extent of what was done.
The muster list sets the duties assigned in each drill.
Drills are the occasion on which most LSA defects are actually found — raise them as deficiencies, do not close the drill and forget them.
Liberia Marine Notice SAF-004 addresses drills.

flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-004 covers drills.

title: Abandon-ship drill content
what: The abandon-ship drill exercises the muster, the boat and raft preparation, the launching arrangements and the survival equipment the crew would actually use.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, drill record
detailBullets: Summon the crew with the general emergency alarm and the public address announcement.
Report to stations and prepare for the duties described in the muster list.
Check that everyone is suitably dressed and that lifejackets are correctly donned.
Operate the davits used for launching, and inspect and operate the survival craft as required by the regulation.
Record what was actually done — a generic entry is not evidence.

title: Fire drill content
what: The fire drill exercises the fire party, the fire main, the fixed and portable appliances and the closing of openings, using different scenarios in different parts of the ship.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, drill record
detailBullets: Report to stations and prepare for the duties in the muster list.
Start a fire pump using at least the required number of jets to show the system is in order.
Check the fireman's outfits and other personal rescue equipment.
Check the relevant communication equipment, the operation of watertight doors, fire doors, fire dampers and the main inlets and outlets of ventilation systems.
Vary the scenario so that different spaces and different equipment are exercised.

title: Survival craft — carriage requirements
what: The ship carries survival craft of the types and capacities required for its type, size and trade, stowed so they can be launched in the required time.
howOften: At survey and on any change
evidence: Safety Equipment Certificate and Record of Equipment
detailBullets: The Record of Equipment attached to the Safety Equipment Certificate is the authoritative list of what the ship must carry.
Survival craft capacity, stowage position and embarkation arrangements are fixed by the approved plans.
Substituting a craft or moving a stowage position needs the Administration's or the RO's agreement.
Check the Record of Equipment against the register in this app when joining the ship — that reconciliation catches most register errors.
The maintenance regime that follows is in SOLAS III/20.

title: Rescue boats — carriage and readiness
what: The ship carries at least one rescue boat, ready for launching in the required time, with a trained crew assigned in the muster list.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, drill record
detailBullets: A lifeboat may be accepted as a rescue boat where it also meets the rescue boat requirements.
The rescue boat crew is named in the muster list and exercised in the drills.
The launching appliance follows the same MSC.402(96) task set as a lifeboat davit.
Anti-exposure suits for the rescue boat crew are part of the outfit.
Recovery arrangements for a person in the water are exercised with the boat.

title: Embarkation and launching arrangements
what: Embarkation stations, ladders and lighting are arranged so that the survival craft can be boarded and launched safely under the conditions the regulation assumes.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: Embarkation ladders are rigged at the stations shown on the plans and are inspected monthly.
Lighting at the embarkation station and over the water is supplied from the emergency source of power.
Access routes to the stations are kept clear of stores, lashings and deck cargo.
The muster station marking and the escape route signs form part of the same arrangement.

title: Lifebuoys — number, marking and equipment
what: The ship carries the required number of lifebuoys, marked with the ship's name and port of registry, distributed on both sides and fitted with lights, smoke signals and buoyant lines as required.
detailBullets: Lifebuoys are so placed as to be readily available on both sides of the ship and, so far as practicable, on all open decks extending to the ship's side.
At least one lifebuoy on each side is fitted with a buoyant lifeline.
Lifebuoys with self-igniting lights and self-activating smoke signals are quick-release from the bridge wings.
Lifebuoys are not permanently secured — a lashing is a finding.
Retro-reflective tape and the ship's name marking are checked monthly.

title: Lifejackets — number, stowage and marking
what: A lifejacket is provided for every person on board, with additional jackets for watchkeepers and for remotely located stations, plus child and infant jackets where carried.
detailBullets: Lifejackets are stowed so as to be readily accessible and their position is clearly indicated.
Additional lifejackets are provided for persons on watch and for use at remotely located survival craft stations.
Lifejacket lights and whistles are fitted; the light battery expiry is the date most often missed.
Donning instructions are posted at the stowage.
Inflatable lifejackets are serviced annually — see the servicing card.

flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-006 covers lifejackets.

title: Immersion suits and thermal protective aids
what: Immersion suits are provided for every person on board (and for the rescue boat crew where required), with thermal protective aids in the survival craft.
howOften: Monthly inspection; air-pressure test per flag
detailBullets: Suits are stowed where they can be reached and donned quickly, and their position is marked.
Zips are exercised and lubricated and the seals are examined at the monthly inspection.
The air-pressure test regime is set by the flag Administration — check the FLAG section.
Thermal protective aids are part of the survival craft inventory and have their own count.
Suits that fail the test are landed, not stowed back in the locker.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: immersion suits less than 10 years old tested at intervals not exceeding 3 years.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-007 covers immersion suits and TPAs.

title: Distress signals — rockets, hand flares and smoke signals
what: The ship carries the required outfit of rocket parachute flares on the bridge and the pyrotechnic items in the survival craft inventories, all within their marked expiry.
detailBullets: Read the expiry from the item — this app never assumes a shelf life.
Expired signals are landed ashore against a receipt and are not stowed with the in-date stock.
Signals are kept in a watertight container at the stowage position.
The survival craft inventories have their own pyrotechnic counts — check them together.
Plan renewal before the expiry month: supply in some ports is slow.

title: General emergency alarm and public address system
what: The general emergency alarm sounds throughout the accommodation, the normal crew working spaces and the open decks, and is supplemented by a public address system.
detailBullets: The alarm is capable of being sounded from the navigation bridge.
It continues to sound until manually switched off or interrupted by the public address announcement.
The system operates from the emergency source of power.
The weekly test is one of the three weekly LSA items and is logged.
Audibility over machinery noise and in cabins is the usual failure — test both.

title: Muster list and emergency instructions
what: Clear instructions for every person on board are provided, and muster lists are posted in conspicuous places showing duties, alarm signals and the action to take.
detailBullets: The muster list shows the duties assigned to each crew member and the substitutes for key persons.
It specifies the general emergency alarm signal and the action to take on hearing it.
It is posted before the ship sails and is updated whenever the crew changes.
It is in the working language of the ship.
Illustrated instructions are posted in cabins and at the muster stations.

title: Life-saving appliance training manual
what: A training manual covering the ship's life-saving appliances and the best method of survival is provided in each mess room and recreation room, in the working language of the ship.
detailBullets: The manual explains the use of every appliance actually fitted.
It covers donning of lifejackets and immersion suits, muster and abandon-ship procedures, survival at sea and the use of the radio life-saving appliances.
It is in the working language of the ship.
Onboard training records reference the manual.
Replace the manual when appliances are changed.

title: Satellite EPIRB — carriage, testing and maintenance
what: The ship carries a float-free satellite EPIRB, correctly registered, with its battery and hydrostatic release within their marked dates and an annual performance test recorded.
howOften: Annual performance test; battery and HRU per maker
detailBullets: The EPIRB is installed so that it floats free and activates automatically.
Battery expiry and hydrostatic release expiry are separate dates — record both.
Registration details are updated on any change of owner, ship name or contact.
The annual performance test is carried out using the unit's self-test function or as the maker directs; a shore-based maintenance test is carried out at the interval the Administration requires.
Do not test-transmit on the live frequency.

title: Search and rescue locating device (SART / AIS-SART)
what: The ship carries search and rescue locating devices, stowed so they can be taken into a survival craft, with the batteries in date and a self-test recorded.
detailBullets: The device is stowed where it can be rapidly placed in a survival craft.
Battery expiry is marked on the unit — record it.
Carry out the self-test as the maker directs; do not radiate on the live frequency unnecessarily.
Bracket and lanyard are checked with the unit.
The number required depends on the ship's size — check the Record of Equipment.

title: Two-way VHF radiotelephone apparatus for survival craft
what: The ship carries the required number of two-way VHF radiotelephones for survival craft, with sealed primary batteries in date and rechargeable sets kept charged.
detailBullets: The sets are stowed so they can be rapidly placed in any survival craft.
Sealed primary batteries for emergency use carry their own expiry date.
Where a rechargeable battery is fitted, a spare sealed battery is also provided.
The sets are function tested monthly on a working channel, not on the distress channel.
The number required depends on the ship's size — check the Record of Equipment.

title: Pilot transfer arrangements
what: Pilot ladders and their associated equipment are of an approved type, correctly rigged, certified and inspected, and are used only for pilot transfer.
detailBullets: The ladder is certified and the certificate is kept on board.
Steps are horizontal, of equal spacing, not painted over and not secured with shackles or knots.
Spreader steps are fitted at the required intervals.
A lifebuoy with a self-igniting light, a heaving line and man-ropes are ready at the point of access.
The ladder is secured to the ship's side by the approved arrangement, not by rope lashings.

title: Chapter V items that touch the LSA and FFE register
what: Some Chapter V equipment — signalling lamps, navigational and communication arrangements — is inspected on the same rounds as the LSA and FFE and is carried in the register for convenience.
detailBullets: The daylight signalling lamp must operate from a source of power independent of the ship's main supply.
Man-overboard and pilot transfer arrangements are checked alongside the LSA.
Items recorded here for convenience are still governed by their own regulation — this card is a pointer, not the requirement.
Keep the Record of Equipment to hand when reconciling the register.

title: Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate and Record of Equipment
what: The Safety Equipment Certificate and its Record of Equipment state what life-saving and fire-fighting equipment the ship is required to carry, and its expiry drives the survey programme.
detailBullets: The Record of Equipment is the authoritative list — reconcile the register against it.
The certificate expiry date drives the 'due before next survey' view in this app.
The harmonised survey window is the anniversary date ±3 months for the items to which it applies.
Endorsements for annual and intermediate surveys are made on the certificate.
An item landed for service must be recorded and its absence explained at the survey.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 sets a ±3-month window on annual LSA performance tests.

title: Company and Master responsibilities for maintenance records
what: The safety management system defines who maintains the LSA and FFE, how the maintenance is planned and recorded, and how deficiencies are reported and closed out.
evidence: SMS procedures, maintenance records, non-conformity reports
detailBullets: The maintenance regime in this app must match the vessel's own SMS planned maintenance system — the SMS prevails.
Deficiencies found on rounds are raised, reported and closed out through the SMS.
Records are retained for the period the SMS specifies.
The Master's authority to take action in the interest of safety is not limited by any planning tool.
DeckWatch does not discharge any obligation under SOLAS or the ISM Code.

title: Operational readiness and maintenance of fire protection systems
what: Fire protection systems and fire-fighting systems and appliances are kept in good order and ready for immediate use, under a maintenance plan kept on board.
detailBullets: The maintenance plan is kept on board and is available for inspection.
It covers the fire main, fixed systems, portable appliances, detection and alarm, structural fire protection and the fireman's outfits.
For tankers the plan includes additional items such as the inert gas and deck foam systems.
MSC.1/Circ.1432 as amended gives the guidelines for the maintenance and inspection regimes.
Panama requires the plan to state which tasks are crew-performed and which need specially trained persons.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice FIR-001 covers fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Operational readiness — what 'ready for immediate use' means in practice
what: Every appliance is in its designated position, accessible, complete, in date and capable of being used by the crew without preparation.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: Access to appliances is not obstructed by stores, lashings or deck cargo.
An appliance landed for service is replaced by a spare or its absence is formally recorded.
Isolated systems, closed valves and disabled detection zones are entered in the defect log and restored as soon as possible.
Instructions are posted where the appliance is used and are legible.
Readiness is what PSC tests — usually by asking a rating to fetch and use an item.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire fighting — arrangements and appliances
what: The ship is provided with the fire main, hydrants, hoses, nozzles, portable appliances, fixed systems and fireman's outfits required for its type and size.
howOften: At survey; per the onboard maintenance plan
detailBullets: The Record of Equipment attached to the Safety Equipment Certificate lists what must be carried.
Fire pumps, the fire main, hydrants, hoses and nozzles form the water fire-fighting system.
Portable and mobile appliances are distributed as shown on the fire control plan.
Fixed systems protect machinery spaces, cargo spaces and other high-risk areas.
Fireman's outfits and EEBDs complete the personnel protection arrangements.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice FIR-001 covers fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Portable fire extinguishers — provision and spare charges
what: Portable fire extinguishers of suitable types and capacity are provided in the accommodation, service and control spaces and the machinery spaces, with spare charges or spare extinguishers as required.
detailBullets: One extinguisher is located near the entrance to each space it protects.
Spare charges are provided for extinguishers that can be recharged on board; where they cannot be recharged, additional extinguishers are provided instead.
The extinguishing medium must be suited to the risk in the space.
Each appliance is marked with its instructions and shown on the fire control plan.
The monthly check and the annual service are the two dates PSC will look for.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001 allows trained ship's crew to carry out the annual servicing.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire main, pumps, hydrants and hoses
what: The fire main is capable of supplying the required number of jets at the required pressure, with the main and emergency fire pumps, isolating valves and the international shore connection.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; at survey
detailBullets: Record the pressure achieved at the most remote hydrant with the required number of jets.
Isolating valves allow a damaged length of main to be cut out — their positions are on the fire control plan.
The emergency fire pump is in its own space with an independent supply.
The international shore connection is available on both sides of the ship.
Hoses are connected in accommodation and service spaces and are pressure tested at the plan's interval.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fixed fire-extinguishing systems
what: Machinery spaces, cargo spaces and other protected spaces are served by fixed fire-extinguishing systems of an approved type, with release controls outside the protected space.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; 2-yearly content check
detailBullets: Release controls are grouped outside the protected space with clear operating instructions.
A pre-discharge alarm and the means of stopping ventilation and fuel supply are part of the arrangement.
Content checks, hose replacement and cylinder testing are provider tasks — see the FFE cards.
The system is shown on the fire control plan with the protected spaces marked.
Never leave a system isolated after maintenance without a defect entry and a plan to restore it.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14: fixed-gas cylinders to hold not less than 95% of the nominal charge.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001: fixed CO2 cylinders to hold not less than 90% of the nominal charge.

title: Fixed fire detection and fire alarm systems
what: Accommodation, service spaces, control stations and machinery spaces are protected by a fixed fire detection and fire alarm system with indication at a continuously manned station.
evidence: Signed checklist, panel record, Service report
detailBullets: The panel indicates the zone or address of the detector in alarm.
Detectors are of a type suited to the space — smoke, heat, flame or a combination.
A sample of detectors and call points is tested monthly; all detectors are tested at 5-yearly intervals by a service facility.
Standing faults and disablements are recorded and cleared, not normalised.
Spare detector heads and the test equipment are carried on board.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fireman's outfits and personal equipment
what: The ship carries the required number of fireman's outfits, complete with protective clothing, boots, gloves, helmet, safety lamp, axe, fire-resistant lifeline and breathing apparatus, stowed widely separated.
detailBullets: Outfits are stowed in widely separated positions so that a single fire cannot deny access to all of them.
Two spare charges are provided for each required breathing apparatus, or the ship has means of recharging on board.
The safety lamp must operate for the duration required by the FSS Code.
The axe has an insulated handle.
Cylinder pressures are checked weekly and verified by the responsible officer monthly.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Emergency escape breathing devices (EEBD)
what: EEBDs are provided in the accommodation and machinery spaces at the locations shown on the fire control plan, for escape only.
detailBullets: An EEBD is for escape from a space with a hazardous atmosphere — never for fire fighting or for enclosed space entry.
Units are located so that they can be reached on the escape route, and their positions are on the fire control plan.
The pressure indicator is checked at the plan's interval and the seal must be intact.
Training units are clearly marked and kept apart from the service units.
Cylinders are hydrostatically tested at the same 5-year interval as SCBA cylinders.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Means of escape, marking and low-location lighting
what: Escape routes are kept clear and are marked with signs and low-location lighting so they can be followed with the lights out and in smoke.
detailBullets: Escape routes are not obstructed by stores, furniture or work in progress.
Signs and arrows point along the route that is actually available.
Low-location lighting is continuous along the route in the accommodation.
Escape trunks from machinery spaces are kept clear and their doors operable from inside.
Signs come from the escape route sign standard — see the symbol cards.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-10 covers fire control plans, escape route signs and lifesaving symbols.

title: Fire doors and closing appliances in fire divisions
what: Doors in A- and B-class divisions are self-closing or capable of remote release, and are kept closed or capable of closing at all times.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: A self-closing door must never be wedged, hooked or tied open.
Power-operated sliding doors are tested locally and from the remote release position.
Door seals, hinges and closers are maintained; holes cut for cables destroy the division.
The doors and their class are shown on the fire control plan.
This is the single most common structural fire protection finding at PSC.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Structural fire protection — divisions and penetrations
what: The integrity of A- and B-class divisions is maintained, including at penetrations for cables, pipes and ducts.
detailBullets: Any new penetration must be made good to the standard of the division.
Insulation removed for maintenance is reinstated in full.
Fire dampers, closing appliances and doors form part of the division.
The main vertical zones and division classes are shown on the fire control plan.
Record modifications so the fire control plan can be updated.

title: Ventilation closing appliances and remote stops
what: Ventilation openings serving machinery and cargo spaces can be closed from outside the space, and the fans can be stopped from grouped, marked remote positions.
detailBullets: Closing appliances, dampers and skylights are exercised and must not be seized with paint.
The remote stops must stop every fan serving the space, not only the main supply fan.
Controls are grouped in as few positions as possible and are clearly marked.
Prove the stop at the fan, not only at the control panel.
The arrangement is essential before releasing a fixed gas system.

title: Fuel and lubricating oil shut-off arrangements
what: Quick-closing valves on oil tanks and remote stops for oil pumps can be operated from outside the space they serve, from grouped and marked positions.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: Quick-closing valves are tested and always re-set afterwards — a valve left tripped is a serious defect.
Remote stops cover transfer, service, booster and purifier feed pumps.
Wires, pulleys and pneumatic lines are maintained free and greased.
The positions are marked and shown on the fire control plan.
Record every test — this is a routine survey demonstration.

title: Galley ranges, hoods and exhaust ducts
what: Galley exhaust ducts and range hoods are fitted with grease traps, fire dampers and a fixed extinguishing arrangement, and are cleaned at the plan's interval.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; cleaning per plan
detailBullets: Grease build-up in the hood and duct is the fire risk — record the cleaning.
The manual release for the hood system must be accessible, not blocked by galley equipment.
The arrangement includes shutting off the fuel or power to the range on release.
A fire blanket is provided at the galley.
The duct damper is exercised with the other dampers.

title: Inert gas systems on tankers
what: Tankers to which the requirement applies are fitted with an inert gas system capable of maintaining the cargo tank atmosphere below the required oxygen content.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; at survey
detailBullets: The oxygen analyser is calibrated at the maker's interval and the calibration gas has its own expiry.
Deck seal, non-return valve, alarms and shutdowns are tested and recorded.
The system is examined at the Safety Equipment survey and is a standing PSC focus item.
Operating instructions and the cargo operations manual describe the required oxygen levels.
Failures of the IG plant are recorded and reported as the SMS requires.

title: Fire safety instructions, onboard training and drills
what: Crew members are trained in the ship's fire safety arrangements and take part in fire drills, supported by the fire safety operational booklet and the training manual.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, training record
detailBullets: The fire safety operational booklet describes the arrangements and the action to take.
Onboard training covers the appliances actually fitted, including the fixed systems.
Training in the use of EEBDs stresses that they are for escape only.
Drills exercise different spaces and different equipment in turn.
Training records are kept with the drill records.

title: Fire control plans and their outside container
what: General arrangement plans showing the fire control stations, divisions, detection and extinguishing arrangements are permanently exhibited, and a duplicate set is kept in a weathertight container outside the deckhouse for the shore fire-fighting party.
howOften: Kept current; per the onboard maintenance plan
detailBullets: The plan uses the symbols of the applicable fire control plan symbol standard.
It shows the fire control stations, the divisions of each class, the detection and alarm systems, the extinguishing appliances, the means of access and the ventilation arrangements.
The duplicate set is in a weathertight container outside the deckhouse, marked for the assistance of shore-side fire-fighting personnel.
The plan is kept up to date — modifications must be reflected.
The plan or a booklet is in the working language of the ship.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-10 covers fire control plans, escape route signs and lifesaving symbols.

title: LSA Code Chapter I — general requirements for appliances
what: All life-saving appliances are of an approved type, constructed to the standards of the LSA Code and marked with their approval details.
detailBullets: Appliances are marked with the approval number and the date of manufacture.
Replacement items must be of an approved type and compatible with the installation.
Materials are resistant to deterioration by seawater, oil and sunlight where exposed.
Record the type-approval number in the equipment record — it is asked for at survey.
Where an appliance is replaced with a different make, the maintenance instructions and the provider's authorisation must be updated too.

title: LSA Code Chapter II — personal life-saving appliances
what: Lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits, anti-exposure suits and thermal protective aids meet the construction, marking and performance requirements of Chapter II.
detailBullets: Lifebuoys carry the ship's name and port of registry and are fitted with retro-reflective material.
Lifejackets are fitted with a whistle and a light, with donning instructions posted at the stowage.
Immersion suits are inspected for seal and zip condition and pressure tested to the flag's regime.
Thermal protective aids are part of the survival craft inventories.
Inflatable personal appliances are serviced annually at an approved station or by trained crew where the flag permits.

title: LSA Code Chapter III — visual signals
what: Rocket parachute flares, hand flares and buoyant smoke signals meet the performance requirements of Chapter III and are within their marked expiry.
detailBullets: Each signal is marked with brief instructions or diagrams and with its expiry date.
Signals are carried in a watertight container at the stowage position.
The rocket parachute flare outfit is on the bridge; hand flares and smoke signals are also in the survival craft inventories.
Read the expiry from the item; do not assume a standard shelf life.
Land expired signals ashore against a receipt.

title: LSA Code Chapter IV — survival craft and their equipment
what: Lifeboats and liferafts meet the construction and equipment requirements of Chapter IV, including the item-by-item equipment inventory carried in the craft.
detailBullets: The Chapter IV equipment list is the basis of the boat and raft inventory checklists in this app.
Items with expiry dates — rations, water, pyrotechnics, first-aid kit, batteries — feed the due engine.
Buoyancy, seating capacity and marking are fixed by the approval and shown on the maker's plate.
Engine, steering, drain plugs, painter and boat-hooks are checked with the inventory.
Missing inventory items are the most frequent lifeboat finding at PSC.

title: Lifeboat equipment inventory
what: Each lifeboat carries the full equipment inventory required by the LSA Code, secured within the boat and within its expiry dates.
detailBullets: Check quantities, expiry dates and condition item by item, not by a single tick.
Rations, drinking water, pyrotechnics, first-aid kit and torch batteries all carry dates.
Bailer, buckets, sea anchor, hatchet, boat-hooks, oars and the fishing tackle are counted.
Items are stowed so they cannot move in a seaway and are secured against theft in port.
The compass, the radio equipment and the drinking vessels are part of the same check.

title: Liferaft emergency pack and inventory
what: The liferaft is supplied with the SOLAS A or SOLAS B emergency pack appropriate to the ship's trade, and its contents are renewed at each servicing.
detailBullets: The pack type — SOLAS A or SOLAS B — is stated on the raft container and on the servicing certificate.
Contents and their expiry dates are renewed by the servicing station, not on board.
Confirm the pack type on the certificate matches the ship's trade after any change of trading area.
The container marking shows the capacity, the servicing station and the next service due date.
Keep the servicing certificate with the raft record.

title: LSA Code Chapter V — rescue boats
what: Rescue boats meet the construction, equipment and performance requirements of Chapter V, including the recovery arrangements and the boat's own inventory.
detailBullets: The boat is capable of being launched and recovered in the conditions the Code assumes.
Inflated rescue boats have their own inflation-chamber and pressure checks in the maker's manual.
The boat's engine is run weekly with the lifeboat engines.
Anti-exposure suits for the crew are part of the outfit.
The launching appliance follows the MSC.402(96) task set.

title: LSA Code Chapter VI — launching and embarkation appliances
what: Davits, winches, falls, release gear and embarkation arrangements meet the requirements of Chapter VI and are examined and tested to MSC.402(96).
evidence: Signed checklist, Service report, Statement of fitness
detailBullets: The launching appliance operates by gravity or by stored mechanical power independent of the ship's power supply.
The winch brake holds the boat with its full complement and equipment.
On-load release gear is designed so that it cannot release until the boat is waterborne.
Falls, sheaves and limit switches are examined at the annual thorough examination.
Embarkation ladders and the lighting at the station are part of the arrangement.

title: LSA Code Chapter VII — other life-saving appliances
what: Line-throwing appliances, general alarm and public address systems meet the requirements of Chapter VII.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: The line-throwing appliance is capable of throwing a line with reasonable accuracy at the range the Code requires.
Rockets and lines both carry expiry dates — record whichever is earlier.
The general emergency alarm and the public address system are tested weekly.
The public address system overrides local volume controls and operates on emergency power.
Alarm audibility in cabins with the door shut is the usual failure point.

title: MSC.402(96) — scope of the maintenance, examination and testing regime
what: MSC.402(96) sets the requirements for the maintenance, thorough examination, operational testing, overhaul and repair of lifeboats, rescue boats, launching appliances and release gear.
detailBullets: It distinguishes the inspections that ship's personnel carry out from the examinations that require an authorised service provider.
It requires the provider to be authorised for the specific make and type of equipment.
It covers lifeboats, rescue boats, fast rescue boats, launching appliances and on-load release gear.
The annual thorough examination and the five-yearly tests are the two provider milestones.
The reports and statements of fitness are kept on board with the maintenance records.

title: Annual thorough examination and operational test of survival craft and launching appliances
what: Once every 12 months, with the HSSC window of ±3 months, the survival craft, its launching appliance and its on-load release gear are thoroughly examined and operationally tested by an authorised service provider or the manufacturer.
evidence: Service report, Statement of fitness, Certificate
detailBullets: The provider must be authorised for the make and type of equipment on board — check the authorisation before the job, not after.
The examination covers the craft, the davit structure, the winch and brake, the falls, the sheaves, the limit switches and the release gear.
The operational test includes lowering and recovering the craft as the resolution requires.
A statement of fitness is issued on completion and kept on board.
The examination is planned inside the HSSC window so it aligns with the Safety Equipment survey.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: reports countersigned by the Company representative or the Master.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-005 — use a provider from the Administration's published list.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-258 governs authorised service providers; MMC-281 gives a ±3-month window on annual LSA performance tests.

title: Five-yearly overload operational test and winch brake dynamic test
what: Every 5 years the on-load release gear is overhauled and subjected to an overload operational test at 1.1 times the fully-loaded mass of the craft, and the winch brake is given a dynamic test.
evidence: Service report, test Certificate, Statement of fitness
detailBullets: The overload test load is 1.1 times the fully-loaded mass of the survival craft with its full complement and equipment.
The release gear is overhauled at the same time.
The winch brake dynamic test is carried out by the authorised provider.
Record the fully-loaded mass in the equipment attributes so the test load can be stated.
Some Administrations require an RO surveyor to attend.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: the five-yearly overload test and overhaul is carried out with an RO surveyor in attendance.

title: Authorisation of service providers for survival craft and launching appliances
what: The firm carrying out the annual examination and the five-yearly tests must be authorised for the specific make and type of the equipment, and its technicians certified accordingly.
detailBullets: Ask for the authorisation certificate and check the makes and types listed on it.
IACS UR Z17 governs the approval of service suppliers to class.
A service supplier may certify only its own employees unless the flag approves otherwise.
Flags publish their own requirements and, in some cases, lists of accepted providers.
File the authorisation with the service report — a surveyor may ask for both.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Technical Circular 1 covers shipboard equipment and service provider approvals.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia publishes a list of authorised lifeboat service providers (Marine Notice SAF-005).
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-258 lists authorised service providers; provider certificates are valid 3 years.

title: Approval of servicing stations for inflatable liferafts
what: Inflatable liferafts are serviced only at a servicing station approved under the recommendation in Resolution A.761(18).
detailBullets: The station must be approved for the make of raft it services.
The servicing certificate states the station, the date, the raft serial number and the next service due date.
Ask the station to return the old certificate with the new one so the history is continuous.
Where a raft is landed, record it as landed ashore so the register does not show it on board.
Marine evacuation systems are serviced under equivalent arrangements.

title: Immersion suits — maintenance and testing guidance
what: Immersion suits are inspected and air-pressure tested in accordance with the guidance in MSC/Circ.1047, at the intervals the flag Administration applies.
howOften: Per flag; 3 years for suits under 10 years old
detailBullets: The seam and closure air-pressure test is the practical way of proving a suit is still watertight.
Suits under 10 years old are commonly tested at intervals not exceeding 3 years — confirm against your flag's notice.
Zips are exercised and lubricated with the maker's recommended lubricant.
A suit that fails is landed and replaced, not returned to the locker.
Record the test date per stowage location so the whole batch stays in step.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: suits under 10 years old tested at intervals not exceeding 3 years.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-007 covers immersion suits and TPAs.

title: Immersion suits — further guidance on maintenance
what: MSC/Circ.1114 supplements the immersion suit maintenance guidance and is cited by several flag Administrations in their notices.
detailBullets: Use the circular together with the maker's manual and the flag notice.
The person performing the test must be competent and, where the flag requires it, specifically trained.
Record who performed the test as well as the date.
Keep the test equipment calibrated and the procedure available.
Where the flag requires the test to be done ashore, plan it against the port rotation.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37 refers to the immersion suit testing regime.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-007 covers immersion suits and TPAs.

title: Onboard maintenance instructions for life-saving appliances
what: Instructions for onboard maintenance of the life-saving appliances are provided and are easily understood, illustrated where possible, and include the checklists used for the monthly inspection.
detailBullets: The instructions cover every appliance fitted, including the launching appliances and the release gear.
They include checklists, servicing schedules, a troubleshooting guide and a maintenance record.
Where a planned maintenance programme is used instead, it must cover the same ground.
Replace the instructions when equipment is changed.
The signed checklists are the evidence of the monthly inspection.

title: On-load release gear — operation, examination and overhaul
what: The on-load release gear is maintained so that it releases only when the boat is waterborne, resets correctly, and is examined annually and overload tested every 5 years.
evidence: Signed checklist, Service report, Statement of fitness
detailBullets: The hydrostatic interlock must prevent on-load release while the boat is out of the water.
The reset indicator must show clearly that the hooks are correctly reset.
The maker's operating instructions are posted in the boat.
Only a provider authorised for this make and type may examine and test the gear.
Accidental release during drills is the classic cause of lifeboat casualties — never defeat the interlock.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: RO surveyor in attendance at the five-yearly overload test and overhaul.

title: Davits and winches — examination, brake tests and lubrication
what: Davits, winches and their brakes are maintained, examined annually and given a dynamic brake test every 5 years by an authorised provider.
detailBullets: Sheaves, pivot pins and bearings are greased at the interval in the maintenance instructions.
Limit switches are proved to operate — never bypassed for convenience.
The brake band and lining are examined for wear and oil contamination.
Remote brake release wires are checked free and correctly adjusted.
The winch foundation and davit pedestal are checked for corrosion at the deck.

title: Falls and wire terminations
what: Falls are maintained, inspected weekly, examined annually, turned end-for-end and renewed at the intervals in SOLAS III/20 and the maker's instructions.
howOften: Weekly inspection; end-for-end and renewal per SOLAS III/20
evidence: Log book entry, signed, wire certificate
detailBullets: Inspect at the sheave contact zones and at the terminations, where deterioration starts.
Record the fitting, end-for-end and renewal dates with the wire certificate number.
Some Administrations do not accept bulldog grips on load-bearing terminations.
Lubricate with the maker's recommended dressing, not with ordinary grease.
A wire with broken strands, corrosion or a kink is renewed regardless of its age.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: bulldog grips prohibited on load-bearing wire terminations.

title: Fall preventer devices
what: Where a fall preventer device is used as a risk-control measure during drills, it is fitted, inspected and removed in accordance with the vessel's approved procedure and the maker's instructions.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: An FPD is a risk-control measure, not a substitute for correctly maintained release gear.
The device, strop and shackles are of known provenance and are inspected before use.
Fitting and removal are part of the drill procedure and are briefed.
Record its inspection with the boat's monthly checklist.
Follow the vessel's SMS procedure — practice differs between operators.

title: Survival craft engines — weekly run and maintenance
what: The lifeboat and rescue boat engines are run weekly, kept fuelled with fresh fuel, and maintained in accordance with the maker's instructions.
detailBullets: Run the engine for the period stated in the maintenance instructions.
Demonstrate ahead and astern where the installation allows.
Confirm cooling water flow and check for exhaust leaks into the boat.
Keep the fuel tank full and renew the fuel at the maker's interval — stale fuel is the usual cause of a failed start.
Keep the batteries charged and the terminals clean; record the battery renewal date.

title: Lifeboat water spray (sprinkler) and air support systems
what: Lifeboats fitted with a water spray system and an air support system have both proved at the annual thorough examination and checked on the monthly round.
detailBullets: The spray system draws from the sea and must be proved to deliver over the whole canopy.
Nozzles are easily painted over — check them every month.
The air support cylinders carry pressure and hydrostatic test dates.
The boat's door and hatch seals must hold the internal overpressure.
Both systems are exercised at the annual thorough examination.

title: Hydrostatic release units, painters and weak links
what: The liferaft float-free arrangement — HRU, painter and weak link — is rigged to the maker's diagram, checked monthly and renewed at the marked expiry.
howOften: Monthly check; HRU 24 months or per maker
detailBullets: Read the expiry stamped on the HRU — it is the date, not the fitting date, that governs.
The painter must lead to the weak link so the raft is released when the ship sinks.
The senhouse slip and cradle must be free to render — paint is the usual failure.
A raft lashed with a solid shackle instead of the weak link cannot float free.
Disposable units are replaced at 24 months; serviceable units go to an approved station.

title: Lifebuoys, lights, smoke signals and buoyant lines
what: Lifebuoys and their attachments are complete, marked, in date and immediately available on both sides of the ship.
detailBullets: Lifebuoys are never permanently secured — quick-release brackets must render.
Self-igniting lights carry a battery expiry; self-activating smoke signals carry their own expiry.
The buoyant line lifebuoy must have its line free to run.
The ship's name and port of registry marking is checked for legibility.
Bridge-wing lifebuoys must be releasable from the bridge in a man-overboard situation.

title: Lifejackets, lights and whistles
what: Lifejackets are complete with lights and whistles, in date, stowed accessibly with donning instructions posted, and in sufficient number for everyone on board.
detailBullets: Count them against the persons on board plus the watchkeeping and remote-station extras.
Lifejacket light batteries carry an expiry — renew the batch together.
Whistles and their lanyards are checked with the jackets.
Donning instructions are posted at every stowage.
Inflatable jackets are serviced annually and carry a service label.

flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-006 covers lifejackets.

title: Immersion suits and anti-exposure suits — care and testing
what: Immersion suits are kept clean, dry, with zips lubricated and seals sound, and are pressure tested at the interval the flag Administration requires.
detailBullets: Suits are stowed at the muster station and at the watch stations, not in a store room.
Exercise and lubricate the zip at every monthly inspection.
Inspect the face, wrist and ankle seals for perishing and the retro-reflective tape for adhesion.
Record the pressure test date per stowage location.
Land failed suits ashore — do not return them to the locker.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-37: suits under 10 years old tested at intervals not exceeding 3 years.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice SAF-007 covers immersion suits and TPAs.

title: Thermal protective aids
what: Thermal protective aids are carried in the numbers required in the survival craft and at the muster stations, sealed and undamaged.
detailBullets: Counted as part of the survival craft equipment inventory.
Bags are checked sealed, dry and undamaged.
Replace any aid whose bag has split — damp contents are useless.
Include them in the abandon-ship drill familiarisation.
Record quantity per stowage location.

title: Pyrotechnics — stowage, expiry and disposal
what: Pyrotechnic signals are stowed in watertight containers at their designated positions, checked monthly and renewed at the marked expiry.
detailBullets: Record the expiry from the item — the app never assumes a shelf life.
Keep expired stock apart from in-date stock, and land it ashore against a receipt.
Watertight containers are checked for seals and drainage.
Count the bridge outfit and the survival craft outfits separately.
Order replacements early — availability in some ports is poor.

title: Line-throwing appliance
what: The line-throwing appliance and its rockets and lines are carried in the required number, stowed dry and renewed at their marked expiry.
detailBullets: Rockets and lines carry separate expiry dates — the earlier date governs.
The appliance and its outfit are stowed together in a watertight container.
Instructions for use are with the appliance and are legible.
Familiarisation with the appliance is part of the drill programme.
Land expired rockets ashore against a receipt.

title: EPIRB — dates, registration and float-free arrangement
what: The EPIRB is registered, mounted so it floats free, and has its battery, hydrostatic release and annual performance test all within date.
detailBullets: Three dates to track: battery expiry, hydrostatic release expiry, annual performance test.
Confirm the float-free path is clear and the bracket is not painted solid.
Registration must be updated on any change of owner, ship name, flag or contact.
Carry out the self-test as the maker directs; do not transmit on the live frequency.
Shore-based maintenance testing is done at the interval the Administration requires.

title: SART / AIS-SART — stowage, battery and self-test
what: Search and rescue locating devices are stowed for rapid transfer to a survival craft, with batteries in date and self-tests recorded.
detailBullets: Battery expiry is marked on the unit; record it and renew before it expires.
The bracket must allow the unit to be removed quickly with the lanyard attached.
Perform the self-test per the maker's instructions.
Record the number carried against the Record of Equipment.
Familiarise the crew with taking the SART to the boat in the abandon-ship drill.

title: Two-way VHF radiotelephones for survival craft
what: The survival craft VHF sets are carried in the required number, stowed for rapid transfer, with sealed primary batteries in date.
detailBullets: Sealed primary batteries for emergency use carry an expiry — record it per set.
Where a rechargeable battery is used for routine work, a spare sealed battery is also carried.
Function test on a working channel, not on the distress channel.
Sets are stowed together where they can be taken to any survival craft.
The number required depends on the ship's size — check the Record of Equipment.

title: Marine evacuation systems
what: A marine evacuation system is serviced and deployment tested at the intervals set by the maker and the flag Administration, by an approved station.
howOften: Servicing 12 months; deployment test per maker and flag
evidence: Servicing certificate, deployment test Service report
detailBullets: The system is serviced with its associated liferafts.
Deployment testing follows the maker's programme and the flag's requirement — do not assume an interval.
Container securing and release arrangements are checked on the monthly round.
The embarkation area is kept clear.
Keep the servicing and deployment test records together with the raft certificates.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 provides for extensions up to 17 months for certain inflatable equipment with Administration authorisation.

title: Embarkation ladders
what: Embarkation ladders are provided at the survival craft stations, inspected monthly and rigged so that boarding is possible under the conditions the Code assumes.
detailBullets: Steps and side ropes are inspected for splits, rot and chafe.
The ladder is secured by its approved arrangement at deck level.
It is stowed where it can be rigged quickly, not lashed in a store.
Lighting at the embarkation position is supplied from the emergency source of power.
The ladder is used in drills so the crew know how to rig it.

title: Muster stations — marking, lighting and access
what: Muster (assembly) stations are marked with the standard symbol, adequately lit from the emergency source of power, and reached by clear routes.
detailBullets: The station marking uses the escape-and-assembly symbol set.
Lighting is proved on the emergency source of power, not only on ship's mains.
Access routes are kept clear of stores, lashings and deck cargo.
The muster list assigns persons to each station.
Stations are used as marked in every drill so the crew learn them.

title: International shore connection
what: The ship carries at least one international shore connection to the standard dimensions, with its bolts, nuts, washers and gasket, available on either side of the ship.
detailBullets: The flange dimensions are standard so any shore fire main can be coupled.
Four bolts, eight washers, four nuts and a gasket are supplied with the connection.
It is stowed where it can be brought to either side of the ship.
Its position is shown on the fire control plan.
Missing bolts and gasket are a common and easily avoided finding.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Personnel protection — fireman's outfits, breathing apparatus and EEBDs
what: Fireman's outfits, self-contained breathing apparatus, spare cylinders, fire-resistant lifelines and EEBDs meet the requirements of FSS Code Chapter 3.
detailBullets: The outfit comprises protective clothing, boots, gloves, helmet, safety lamp, axe and a fire-resistant lifeline, plus the breathing apparatus.
Two spare charges are provided for each required apparatus, or the ship can recharge on board.
Breathing air cylinders are hydrostatically tested at 5-yearly intervals at a certified facility.
EEBDs are for escape only and are located as shown on the fire control plan.
The safety lamp must burn for the period the Code requires.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice FIR-001 covers fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire extinguishers — types, capacity, marking and spare charges
what: Portable and wheeled fire extinguishers are of an approved type and capacity, marked with their instructions, and provided with spare charges or replacement appliances.
evidence: Signed checklist, Service report, service label
detailBullets: The extinguishing medium is matched to the risk in the space it protects.
Each appliance is marked with its instructions for use and its service history label.
Spare charges are provided for appliances that can be recharged on board; otherwise additional appliances are carried.
CO2 extinguishers are not used in accommodation spaces where the Code restricts them — check the arrangement against the approved plan.
The appliance's own plate gives the tare and charged weights used in the weight check.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001 allows trained ship's crew to carry out the annual servicing as an alternative to a shore facility.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: the maintenance plan must state which tasks are crew-performed (advanced fire-fighting trained) and which need specially trained persons.

title: Fixed gas fire-extinguishing systems
what: Fixed gas systems provide the required quantity of extinguishing medium for the protected space, with release controls, alarms and ventilation shut-off arrangements outside the space.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; 2-yearly content check
detailBullets: Release controls are in an enclosure clearly marked for the protected space.
An audible pre-discharge alarm operates before the medium is released.
Means are provided to close the ventilation and to stop the oil supply to the space.
The quantity of medium is fixed by the space volume — cylinders must not be left short.
The CO2 room itself is ventilated, lit and has an alarm on the door.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14: cylinders to hold not less than 95% of the nominal charge.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001: fixed CO2 cylinders to hold not less than 90% of the nominal charge.

title: Fixed foam fire-extinguishing systems
what: Fixed high-expansion and low-expansion foam systems deliver the required foam quantity and expansion ratio to the protected space.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; analysis per plan
detailBullets: Foam concentrate is periodically sampled and analysed by a laboratory; keep the certificate.
Air inlets to high-expansion generators must be clear.
Proportioners and inductors are function tested at the plan's interval.
The foam type must be compatible with the cargo carried.
Flexible hoses in the system are replaced at 10-yearly intervals.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fixed pressure water-spraying and water-mist systems
what: Fixed pressure water-spraying and water-mist systems deliver the required application rate over the protected area, with the pump, filters and nozzles maintained.
detailBullets: Nozzles must be clear and unpainted — this is the usual defect.
Filters and strainers are cleaned at the maker's interval; water quality matters.
The pump unit must reach and hold its rated pressure.
Section valves are left in the position the operating instructions state.
Local application systems for machinery follow the same maintenance logic.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Automatic sprinkler, fire detection and fire alarm systems
what: The automatic sprinkler system is kept charged and pressurised, with section valves open, alarms proved and spare heads carried.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: The pressure tank level and pressure are checked and recorded.
Each section alarm is proved by opening the test valve.
Sprinkler heads must be unobstructed, unpainted and undamaged.
Spare heads of each type fitted, and the fitting spanner, are carried on board.
The pump starts automatically on a pressure drop — prove it.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fixed fire detection and fire alarm systems
what: The fixed detection and alarm system covers the required spaces, indicates at a continuously manned station and is tested to the maintenance plan.
evidence: Signed checklist, panel record, Service report
detailBullets: The panel identifies the section or address in alarm.
Detector types are matched to the space — smoke, heat, flame or a combination.
Test equipment appropriate to each detector type is carried on board.
Spare detector heads of each type fitted are carried.
Disablements are logged and restored; a standing disablement is a finding.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Sample extraction smoke detection systems
what: Sample extraction smoke detection systems for cargo spaces draw a continuous air sample from each protected space to a detection cabinet.
detailBullets: Sampling pipes are kept clear of cargo dust and water; blockages disable the protection.
Air flow through every sampling pipe is proved, not assumed.
The fan runs continuously while the system is required.
Cabinet indications and alarms are checked monthly.
Where the system also serves as the CO2 injection route, the changeover is proved.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Low-location lighting
what: Low-location lighting marks the escape routes in the accommodation continuously and is visible when the normal lighting fails.
detailBullets: The marking is continuous along the escape route, including at doors and changes of direction.
Photoluminescent material must be charged by the normal lighting — check that lighting changes have not defeated it.
Electrical low-location lighting is supplied from the emergency source of power.
Damaged or removed sections are replaced with material of the same type.
Performance can be checked by darkening the space during a drill.

title: Fixed emergency fire pumps
what: The emergency fire pump is in a space separate from the main machinery space, with an independent source of power and fuel, and is capable of starting and delivering from cold.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; at survey
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: The pump, its source of power and its sea connection are outside the main machinery space.
The independent fuel supply is sufficient for the required running time.
The space is kept heated where freezing is possible, and access is kept clear.
Cold starting and delivery to the fire main is demonstrated at survey and at PSC.
The isolating valve to the fire main must be open or clearly marked for immediate opening.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Arrangement of means of escape
what: Escape routes, trunks, doors and ladders provide ready means of escape from every space, and are marked and kept clear.
detailBullets: Escape trunks from machinery spaces are kept clear of stores.
Escape hatches and doors must open from inside without a tool or a key.
Handrails, ladders and step treads are maintained.
Routes are marked with signs and, in the accommodation, with low-location lighting.
Modifications must not obstruct or lengthen an escape route.

title: Fixed deck foam systems on tankers
what: The deck foam system supplies foam to the cargo deck through monitors and applicators at the required rate, with the concentrate quantity and quality maintained.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; analysis per plan
evidence: Signed checklist, analysis Certificate, Service report
detailBullets: Monitors and applicator connections are exercised so they do not seize.
Foam concentrate is sampled and analysed at the plan's interval; keep the certificate.
The foam main is blown through and drained after any use or test.
The required number of applicators and their branch pipes are stowed on deck.
System capacity is stated in the approved plan — check the tank level against it.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Inert gas systems
what: The inert gas system supplies gas of the required oxygen content to the cargo tanks, with alarms, shutdowns and non-return arrangements maintained and tested.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; at survey
detailBullets: The oxygen analyser is calibrated at the maker's interval; calibration gas carries its own expiry.
The deck seal and the deck non-return valve prevent cargo gas returning to the machinery space.
Alarms and automatic shutdowns are tested and the results recorded.
Fixed and portable oxygen measuring equipment is maintained together.
IG failures are recorded and reported as the SMS and the flag require.

title: Revised guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire protection systems and appliances
what: MSC.1/Circ.1432, as amended, gives the maintenance and inspection regime that the SOLAS II-2/14 onboard maintenance plan is built on.
byWhom: Ship's staff / Authorised service provider / Service facility
detailBullets: It sets out weekly, routine, quarterly, annual, two-yearly, five-yearly and ten-yearly tasks by system.
It distinguishes what the crew may do from what needs a competent person or a service facility.
The vessel's maintenance plan is the local implementation of these guidelines.
Flag Administrations issue their own notices applying and supplementing the circular.
Always work from the current amended text — the circular has been amended.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice FIR-001 covers fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Monthly inspection of portable extinguishers and appliances
what: Every month the portable extinguishers and the other portable appliances are visually inspected in their designated positions.
detailBullets: Confirm the appliance is in its designated position and access is unobstructed.
Check the operating instructions are legible and facing outwards.
Check the safety pin and tamper seal are intact.
Check the pressure gauge or indicator, where fitted, reads in the operating range.
Check the appliance for corrosion, dents and hose or nozzle damage, and the bracket for security.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: the maintenance plan must state which tasks are crew-performed (advanced fire-fighting trained) and which need specially trained persons.

title: Annual servicing of fire extinguishers by a competent person
what: Fire extinguishers are serviced at intervals not exceeding 12 months by a competent person, and the service is recorded on the appliance and in the maintenance records.
detailBullets: 'Competent person' is defined by reference to Resolution A.951(23) guidelines.
Whether trained ship's crew may carry out the annual service is flag-dependent.
The service label shows the date and the identity of the person or company.

CO2 appliances are weighed and dry powder appliances have the powder condition checked as part of the servicing regime — take the specific interval from the maker's manual and the vessel's maintenance plan.
Keep the service report with the equipment record — the label alone is often challenged.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001 allows trained ship's crew (STCW A-VI/3 competence) to carry out the annual servicing as an alternative to a shore facility.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: the maintenance plan must state which tasks are crew-performed (advanced fire-fighting trained) and which need specially trained persons.

title: Five-yearly test discharge of fire extinguishers
what: At five-yearly intervals at least one extinguisher of each type manufactured in the same year is discharged as a test at a service facility.
detailBullets: The sample is one per type and year of manufacture, not one per ship.
Group the fleet of appliances by type and manufacture year so the sample can be planned.
The test is carried out at a service facility, not on board.
Record which appliance was discharged so the sampling history is traceable.
Plan it with the annual service to save a second attendance.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Ten-yearly hydrostatic testing of extinguisher bodies
what: Extinguisher bodies are hydrostatically tested at ten-yearly intervals by a facility certified by a government agency or a recognised organisation.
detailBullets: The manufacture date on the body drives this test — record it.
The test facility must be certified by a government agency or an RO.
The test date is stamped or labelled on the body.
Some makers set an end-of-life earlier than the test interval; follow the shorter.
Plan replacements: hydrostatic testing an old appliance is often uneconomic.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14: the ten-yearly hydrostatic test is to be done by a facility certified by a government agency or an RO.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fixed gas system content checks and flexible hose replacement
what: The content of fixed gas systems is checked at two-yearly intervals, and the system's flexible hoses are replaced at ten-yearly intervals.
detailBullets: Content is checked by weighing or by an approved level-indication method.
Record the result cylinder by cylinder, not as a single system figure.
The minimum acceptable charge percentage is set by the flag — 95% and 90% figures appear in different notices.
Flexible hoses and pilot lines are replaced at ten-yearly intervals.
Distribution pipework is blown through at the interval in the maintenance plan.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14: cylinders to hold not less than 95% of the nominal charge.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001: fixed CO2 cylinders to hold not less than 90% of the nominal charge.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: external technicians must provide an inspection report on completion.

title: Fire detection — monthly sample testing and five-yearly full testing
what: A sample of detectors and manual call points is tested monthly, and all fire detectors are tested at five-yearly intervals by a service facility.
detailBullets: Rotate the monthly sample so that the whole installation is covered over time — record the loop or zone.
Use test equipment appropriate to the detector type: hot air, smoke or aerosol.
The five-yearly test covers every detector and is documented detector by detector.
Manual call points are tested with the detectors.
Fault and disablement records are part of the same evidence pack.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Breathing apparatus — weekly pressure checks and five-yearly cylinder testing
what: Breathing apparatus cylinder pressures are checked weekly with the responsible officer verifying monthly, and the cylinders are hydrostatically tested at five-yearly intervals.
detailBullets: Record the pressure of each set and each spare cylinder weekly.
The responsible officer verifies the records and inspects the sets monthly.
Cylinders are hydrostatically tested every 5 years at a certified facility; the date is stamped on the cylinder.
EEBD cylinders follow the same five-yearly testing interval.
Where the ship recharges on board, the compressor's breathing air quality is tested and certified.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles — inspection and testing
what: The fire main, fire pumps, hydrants, hoses and nozzles are inspected at the plan's interval and tested to the maintenance plan, including a pressure test of the hoses.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; hose testing per plan
detailBullets: Operate each fire pump and record the pressure at the most remote hydrant with the required jets.
Check hydrant valves free, caps and washers fitted, and no leakage under pressure.
Inspect hoses for perforation, rot and coupling damage; test them at the plan's interval.
Check nozzles for the correct type and free changeover.
Include the isolating valves and the international shore connection in the same round.
