flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Maintenance records for fire protection systems
what: Records of the inspections, tests and servicing of the fire protection systems and appliances are kept on board and made available at survey and at port State control.
detailBullets: Records show what was done, when, by whom and with what result.
Service reports from external technicians are filed with the plan.
A missing record is treated as work not done.
Panama expressly allows the records to be paper or computer-based on board.
DeckWatch is a record-keeping aid; the vessel's approved records remain the authority.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia Marine Notice FIR-001 covers fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 allows records to be kept on paper or computer-based on board.

title: Maintenance and inspection of fixed carbon dioxide systems
what: MSC.1/Circ.1318/Rev.1 gives the maintenance and inspection guidelines specific to fixed CO2 fire-extinguishing systems.
howOften: Per the maintenance plan, up to 10-yearly per item
detailBullets: Routine and annual inspections cover the cylinders, connections, pilot lines, distribution pipework and the release station.
The content of the cylinders is verified at the interval in the maintenance plan.
Cylinder hydrostatic testing follows the sampling regime — see the sampling card.
The alarm and ventilation shut-down arrangements are proved.
The CO2 room's own ventilation, lighting and door alarm are part of the inspection.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14: cylinders to hold not less than 95% of the nominal charge.
flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001: cylinders to hold not less than 90% of the nominal charge.

title: CO2 cylinder hydrostatic test sampling
what: CO2 cylinders are hydrostatically tested on a sampling basis: 10% of the bank at 10 years, escalating to 100% at 20 years.
howOften: 10% at 10 years, escalating to 100% at 20 years
detailBullets: Record which cylinders were tested at each sampling so the escalation can be evidenced.
The bank's manufacture date drives the sampling programme.
A cylinder that fails is replaced, and the whole sampling regime is re-examined.
Plan the sampling with the two-yearly content check to save an attendance.
Keep the certificates: the surveyor will want the history, not just the last visit.

title: CO2 release stations, alarms and safety arrangements
what: The release station, its pre-discharge alarm, the ventilation shut-off and the space evacuation arrangements are maintained and tested.
detailBullets: The release cabinet is closed and sealed, with the key in a break-glass box.
Opening the cabinet door sounds the pre-discharge alarm in the protected space.
Operating instructions are posted at the station in the working language.
Ventilation stops and the oil supply is cut before release.
A means of safely evacuating the protected space is part of the arrangement — brief the crew on it.

title: Improved guidelines for marine portable fire extinguishers
what: Resolution A.951(23) gives the guidelines for marine portable fire extinguishers, including the competence expected of the person carrying out the annual service.
detailBullets: The resolution is the reference for what 'competent person' means in the annual service requirement.
It also covers marking, instructions and the arrangements for spare charges.
Flags differ on whether trained ship's crew meet the competence requirement.
Keep the servicing company's competence evidence with the service report.
Read it together with MSC.1/Circ.1432 and FSS Code Chapter 4.

flagNotes.LIB: Liberia FIR-001 allows trained ship's crew (STCW A-VI/3 competence) to carry out the annual servicing.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: the maintenance plan must state which tasks are crew-performed (advanced fire-fighting trained) and which need specially trained persons.

title: Escape route signs and equipment location markings
what: Resolution A.1116(30) is the current IMO symbol standard for escape route signs and equipment location markings, effective from 1 January 2019.
detailBullets: It supersedes A.760(18) and consolidates A.952(23).
Table 1 covers the MES, LSS, EES and FES signs; Table 2 the mandatory-action signs for launching survival craft; Table 3 the SIS fire control plan symbols.
Life-saving and escape signs are green ground with a white symbol; fire-fighting signs are red ground with a white symbol.
Older vessels may still carry the A.952(23) or A.760(18) sets — record which standard the ship uses.
Fire control plan symbols also carry a media colour code.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-10 covers fire control plans, escape route signs and lifesaving symbols.

title: Graphical symbols for shipboard fire control plans (pre-2019 set)
what: Resolution A.952(23) is the pre-2019 fire control plan symbol set, still found on ships built before the current standard took effect.
detailBullets: Record which symbol standard the vessel's plan uses — mixed sets on one plan cause confusion.
A.952(23) has been consolidated into the current standard.
When a plan is redrawn, use the standard current at the time of redrawing.
The media colour code for extinguishing agents is part of the plan symbology.
Do not hand-annotate a plan with symbols from another standard.

title: Symbols related to life-saving appliances and arrangements (superseded set)
what: Resolution A.760(18) was the earlier symbol set for life-saving appliances and arrangements, superseded by the current standard.
detailBullets: Ships built before the current standard may legitimately carry this set.
Replacement signs should follow the standard applicable to the ship, consistently.
Record the standard in use so replacements match.
Do not mix sets along a single escape route.
The colour and shape conventions are common across the sets.

title: ISO 24409 — design and catalogue of shipboard safety signs
what: ISO 24409-1 gives the design principles for shipboard safety signs and ISO 24409-2 the catalogue that assigns the LSS, FES, MES and EES codes.
detailBullets: ISO 24409-2 cross-references the ISO 7010 E-, F-, M-, P- and W-series numbers.
Shape and colour follow ISO 3864-1: green for safe condition, red for fire-fighting, blue for mandatory action, yellow for warning.
The standards are copyright and are sold — artwork is licensed, not free.
When specifying signage, quote the code from the catalogue rather than a description.
This app's symbol library is drawn to the published geometry, not copied from vendor artwork.

title: ISO 7010 safety signs referenced by the shipboard sets
what: ISO 7010 provides the registered safety signs that the shipboard catalogues cross-reference for fire equipment, escape and first aid.
detailBullets: F-series signs cover fire-fighting equipment; E-series cover safe condition and escape.
Using the registered sign keeps the meaning consistent across ships and shore.
Directional arrows have defined rotations — do not invent new ones.
Combine the sign with the supplementary directional arrow rather than redrawing it.
Check the sign is the correct size for its viewing distance.

title: Shipboard plans for fire protection, life-saving appliances and means of escape
what: ISO 17631 gives the requirements for the shipboard plans, harmonised with the shipboard sign catalogue and ISO 7010.
evidence: Fire control, safety and damage control plans
detailBullets: The plan must reflect the ship as fitted — update it after any modification.
Symbol usage on the plan follows the harmonised catalogue.
The plans include the fire control plan, the safety plan and the damage control plan.
Plan legends explain the symbols used, in the working language.
A superseded plan on the bulkhead is a finding even if a current one exists elsewhere.

title: Fire control plan symbols and the media colour code
what: The fire control plan symbol set covers structural divisions, closing appliances, controls, appliances and protected spaces, with a colour code for the extinguishing media.
detailBullets: Media colours: grey for CO2 and nitrogen, brown for other gases, white for powder, yellow for foam, green for water, orange for sprinkler and high-pressure water.
Structural symbols show A-class and B-class divisions and the main vertical zones.
Control symbols show remote releases, ventilation shut-offs, fuel shut-offs and fire pumps.
Protected spaces are marked with the system that serves them.
Keep a legend on the plan — a symbol without a legend is not self-explanatory to a shore fire officer.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-10 covers fire control plans, escape route signs and lifesaving symbols.

title: Wheeled and mobile fire extinguishers
what: Wheeled extinguishers are kept where they can be moved to the risk, with their hose and wheels free, and follow the same service, discharge and hydrostatic regime as portables.
detailBullets: Prove the wheels turn and the route to the risk is clear.
Check the discharge hose for perishing, kinks and blockage.
Cartridge-operated units have their propellant cartridge weighed at the service.
They count towards the required extinguisher provision — check against the Record of Equipment.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281: the maintenance plan must state which tasks are crew-performed (advanced fire-fighting trained) and which need specially trained persons.

title: Hydrants, hoses, nozzles and hose boxes in practice
what: Every hydrant has a hose and dual-purpose nozzle ready for use, valves free, caps and washers fitted, and the hose box complete.
detailBullets: Hoses in accommodation and service spaces are kept connected to the hydrant.
Check for perforation at the folds — the usual failure point.
Blank caps and washers stop the hydrant weeping and freezing.
Record the hose pressure test date against each hose.
Spare couplings, washers and a spanner are carried in the box.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Main fire pumps in practice
what: The main fire pumps deliver the required jets at the required pressure, start on demand including from the remote position, and are recorded as tested.
detailBullets: Record the pressure at the most remote hydrant with the required number of jets — that is the number the surveyor asks for.
Prove the remote start from outside the machinery space.
Clean the sea suction strainers and check the relief valve setting.
Check gland leakage and bearing temperature during the run.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Emergency fire pump in practice
what: The emergency fire pump starts from cold in its own space and delivers to the fire main with the main machinery space isolated.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: Start it cold, without preheating, and time it — that is the PSC test.
Check the independent fuel tank level and that the supply valve is open.
Prove the priming arrangement and the delivery to the fire main.
Keep the space heated, dry, lit and clear — it must not become a store.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: International shore connection in practice
what: The shore connection is complete with bolts, nuts, washers and gasket, stowed ready and marked on the fire control plan.
detailBullets: Keep the fittings bagged with the flange so nothing is lost.
Confirm it can be brought to either side of the ship.
Check the gasket is sound and the flange face undamaged.
Mark its stowage with the standard symbol.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire main and sprinkler section valves
what: Isolating and section valves are exercised, left in their correct position and identified on the fire control plan.
detailBullets: Exercise each valve so it does not seize in position.
Fit and read an identification plate on every valve.
A valve found closed without a reason recorded is a finding.
Sprinkler section valves are secured open and their gauges read correctly.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire and foam monitors
what: Monitors train and elevate freely, are greased at the plan's interval and can reach the areas they are required to protect.
detailBullets: Exercise the training and elevating gear at the plan's interval — they seize quickly on a tanker deck.
Check the nozzle is clear and the drain plug fitted.
Confirm deck cargo does not block the monitor's coverage.
Flush the foam main through after any use.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Foam concentrate — stock, sampling and analysis
what: Foam concentrate is held in the required quantity, sampled and analysed at the plan's interval, and replaced when the analysis fails.
detailBullets: Keep the laboratory analysis certificate with the tank record.
Check the tank level against the quantity in the approved plan.
Look for sediment or separation when sampling.
Use only concentrate compatible with the system and the cargo.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Portable foam applicator units
what: The portable foam applicator, its branch pipe, inductor and concentrate stock are kept together, complete and in date.
detailBullets: Stow the inductor and branch pipe with the concentrate, not in separate lockers.
Check the concentrate containers for damage and the expiry or analysis date.
Confirm the unit can be connected to the nearest hydrant.
Include the applicator in a fire drill so the crew have actually rigged it.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Water fog applicators
what: Water fog applicators are stowed with the fireman's outfits or at the machinery space entrances, clear and undamaged.
detailBullets: Check the nozzle is clear and the lance straight.
Confirm it couples to the ship's hoses.
Mark the stowage position with the standard symbol.
Include it in the fire drill equipment familiarisation.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire blankets
what: Fire blankets are provided at the galley and other cooking positions, in an undamaged container from which the blanket withdraws freely.
detailBullets: Check the pull tabs are present and the container undamaged.
Mount it where it can be reached without passing the risk.
Replace a blanket that has been used — it is not reusable.
Mark the position with the standard symbol.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fire buckets and sand boxes
what: Fire buckets and sand boxes are kept filled, clean and at their designated positions, with the scoop present.
detailBullets: Keep the sand dry — wet, caked sand is useless.
Check the scoop is present and the position marked.
Buckets must not be borrowed for other work.
Positions are shown on the fire control plan.

title: Sprinkler systems in practice
what: The sprinkler system is kept pressurised with section valves open, alarms proved and spare heads carried.
evidence: Signed checklist, Log book entry, signed
detailBullets: Record the pressure tank level and pressure at the plan's interval.
Open each section test valve in turn and confirm the alarm.
Look for heads painted over, obstructed by stores or damaged by cargo work.
Carry spare heads of every type fitted plus the fitting spanner.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Water mist systems in practice
what: The water mist system's pump unit, filters and nozzles are maintained so the system can reach and hold its operating pressure.
detailBullets: Filters and strainers are the usual defect — clean them at the maker's interval.
Confirm nozzle caps are in place and the nozzles clear.
Run the pump unit to its rated pressure at the plan's interval.
Flexible hoses are replaced at ten-yearly intervals.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Dry powder systems on gas carriers
what: The dry powder system's powder charge, propellant pressure, monitors and hand hose lines are maintained ready for immediate use.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; content check per plan
detailBullets: Check the propellant (nitrogen) pressure against the maker's figure.
The powder condition is checked at the interval in the maker's manual.
Exercise the monitors and run out the hand hose lines so they do not seize.
Flexible hoses are replaced at ten-yearly intervals.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Local application fire-fighting systems
what: The local application system protects the specified machinery items, with nozzles correctly aimed and the associated detection operational.
detailBullets: Nozzles displaced during maintenance no longer protect the risk — check the aim.
Keep detection heads clean of oil mist.
Never leave the system isolated after maintenance without a defect entry.
Function test at the interval in the maintenance plan.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Galley hood extinguishing systems
what: The galley hood system, its duct cleaning, manual release and fuel or power shut-off are maintained and tested.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; service per plan
detailBullets: Grease in the hood and duct is the risk — record the cleaning date.
Keep the manual release accessible; galley equipment creeps in front of it.
Confirm the fuel or power to the range is cut on release.
Nozzle caps must be in place so grease does not block the nozzles.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Inert gas system in practice
what: The IG plant's oxygen analyser, deck seal, non-return valve, alarms and shutdowns are maintained, calibrated and tested.
detailBullets: Calibrate the oxygen analyser at the maker's interval; the calibration gas has its own expiry.
Prove the deck seal water supply and the deck non-return valve.
Test the alarms and shutdowns at their set points and record the result.
Record IG failures and the action taken — PSC will ask.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fixed gas detection systems
what: Fixed gas detection for pump rooms and enclosed spaces is calibrated, its sampling lines clear and its alarms proved at the set points.
howOften: Per the onboard maintenance plan; calibration per maker
detailBullets: Calibration gas carries its own expiry — order it before it runs out.
Blocked sampling lines silently disable the protection; prove the flow.
Test the alarms at the set points, not just the panel lamps.
A pump room detector out of service needs a compensating arrangement, recorded.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Portable gas detectors and multi-gas meters
what: Portable meters used for enclosed space entry and hot work are bump tested before use and calibrated at the maker's interval.
howOften: Bump test before use; calibration per maker
detailBullets: Record the bump test — an entry permit signed without one is a finding.
Aspirator hoses and probes perish; check them with the meter.
Keep enough meters for the entry procedure, plus a spare.
Calibration gas expiry is a separate date to track.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: EEBDs in practice
what: EEBDs are in date, sealed, with the pressure indicator in the green, at the positions shown on the fire control plan — for escape only.
detailBullets: An EEBD is never used for fire fighting or enclosed space entry — train the crew on this.
Keep training units clearly marked and separate from the service units.
The cylinder is hydrostatically tested at five-yearly intervals.
Confirm the number and location match the fire control plan.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Fireman's outfits in practice
what: Each outfit is complete, in date, stowed in its designated position widely separated from the others, and can be donned without delay.
detailBullets: Check the outfit item by item: clothing, boots, gloves, helmet, lamp, axe, lifeline, breathing apparatus.
Two spare charges per required apparatus, or the means to recharge on board.
Outfits are stowed widely separated so one fire cannot deny access to all.
The locker must not be locked without the key being immediately available.

flagNotes.RMI: RMI Marine Notice 2-011-14 covers maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.
flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Breathing air compressors
what: Where the ship recharges its own cylinders, the compressor's filters are within their life and the breathing air quality is tested and certified.
howOften: Filter life and air test per maker
detailBullets: Keep the air quality certificate on board with the compressor record.
Change filters by running hours or elapsed time, whichever comes first.
The air intake must be sited clear of engine exhaust and cargo vapours.
Record the running hours so the filter life can be tracked.

flagNotes.PAN: Panama MMC-281 gives guidelines for the maintenance and inspection of fire-protection systems and appliances.

title: Safety lamps for the fireman's outfit
what: The safety lamp operates for the duration the FSS Code requires and its explosion-protection integrity is intact.
detailBullets: Prove the lamp burns for its rated duration, not just that it lights.
A cracked lens destroys the explosion protection — replace the lamp.

title: The Safety Equipment survey cycle — what falls where
what: The Safety Equipment Certificate is maintained by annual, intermediate and renewal surveys, each with a defined scope and a harmonised window.
detailBullets: The harmonised window is the anniversary date ±3 months for the items to which it applies.
Plan provider attendances so they land inside the window, not after it.
Use the Due tab's 'before next survey' view against the certificate expiry to build the shore-service list.
Have the Record of Equipment, the maintenance records and the service reports together before the surveyor arrives.
An item landed for service is recorded as landed, with the expected return date.

title: Annual Safety Equipment survey — what the surveyor looks for
what: At the annual survey the surveyor checks that the equipment listed in the Record of Equipment is on board, in date, maintained and demonstrably operational.
detailBullets: General examination of the LSA and FFE against the Record of Equipment.
Evidence of the weekly and routine routines: log entries and signed checklists.
Liferaft and inflatable servicing certificates in date.
The MSC.402(96) annual thorough examination report and statement of fitness for the survival craft and launching appliances.
Demonstrations: a fire pump, the emergency fire pump from cold, a fire door, a quick-closing valve, the general emergency alarm.
Pyrotechnic and battery expiry dates across the whole outfit.

title: Intermediate Safety Equipment survey — additional scope
what: The intermediate survey covers the annual scope with additional examination of the items the class programme specifies for that point in the certificate cycle.
detailBullets: Expect closer attention to the fixed systems, the detection installation and the structural fire protection.
Five-yearly items falling due around the intermediate are usually planned to it.
Have the fixed gas content check report and the cylinder sampling history to hand.
Confirm the fire control plan reflects any modification since the last survey.
Outstanding conditions of class and memoranda are reviewed.

title: Renewal Safety Equipment survey — full scope
what: The renewal survey is a complete examination of the life-saving and fire-fighting arrangements, with the operational tests and provider evidence for the whole certificate period.
detailBullets: Full examination against the Record of Equipment, item by item.
Five-yearly evidence: release gear overload test, winch brake dynamic test, extinguisher discharge test, full detector test, SCBA cylinder hydrostatic tests.
Ten-yearly evidence: extinguisher hydrostatic tests, fixed system flexible hose replacement, CO2 cylinder sampling.
Complete history of servicing certificates for rafts, lifejackets and HRUs.
Operational demonstration of the fixed systems' release arrangements and alarms.
Prepare with the Survey prep view — everything due before the certificate expiry, split by who must do it.

title: Harmonised survey windows and how to plan against them
what: Items tied to the survey anniversary have a ±3-month window; planning inside it is what keeps the certificate clean.
detailBullets: The window opens 3 months before the anniversary and closes 3 months after it.
Performing early does not move the next anniversary — the anniversary date governs.
Provider availability, not the regulation, is usually the binding constraint.
Build the shore-service list one port ahead, not on arrival.
Panama states a ±3-month window for annual LSA performance tests in its circular.

Approvals are renewed at intervals not exceeding 5 years.
A service supplier may certify only its own employees unless the flag approves otherwise.
Ask for the approval certificate and check the category and the makes covered.

title: Recurring PSC themes — life-saving appliances
what: Port State control inspections repeatedly find the same categories of LSA problem; knowing them lets the officer close them before arrival.
detailBullets: Servicing and examination overdue: liferafts, inflatable lifejackets, the annual thorough examination of boats and davits.
Expired items: pyrotechnics, HRUs, EPIRB batteries, lifejacket lights, immersion suit tests.
Readiness: boats not moved from stowed, engines that will not start, lifebuoys lashed, embarkation routes blocked.
Documentation: missing service reports, unsigned checklists, an out-of-date muster list.
Marking: illegible capacity plates, missing IMO symbols, faded retro-reflective tape.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — fire-fighting equipment
what: The same FFE themes recur across inspection regimes and are almost all closable by the crew before arrival.
detailBullets: Extinguishers: service overdue, gauge outside the operating range, seal or pin missing, access obstructed.
Fire main: hydrant valves seized, caps and washers missing, hoses perished, pressure not demonstrated.
Emergency fire pump: will not start from cold; the space used as a store.
Fixed systems: content check overdue, release cabinet unsealed, alarms inoperative.
Detection: standing disablements, detectors painted or taped over, routine test not recorded.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — portable extinguishers
what: Extinguishers are the most frequently examined FFE item and the easiest to keep clean.
detailBullets: Missing or illegible service label — the inspector's first check.
Pressure gauge outside the operating band on stored-pressure appliances.
Obstructed access, or the appliance removed from its bracket and left on deck.
Missing safety pin or tamper seal.
Hydrostatic test date passed on older appliances.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — lifeboats, davits and release gear
what: Lifeboat findings are the most serious LSA category and can lead to detention.
howOften: Weekly / monthly; before every port call
detailBullets: Annual thorough examination overdue, or the report not for this make and type.
Five-yearly overload test evidence missing.
Engine will not start; batteries flat; fuel stale.
Boat not moved from the stowed position, with no weather entry in the log.
Inventory incomplete — rations, water, flares or first-aid kit missing or expired.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — breathing apparatus and fireman's outfits
what: Breathing apparatus and outfits are examined in most inspections and are frequently found incomplete.
detailBullets: Cylinder pressure below the maker's minimum; spare cylinders not charged.
Cylinder hydrostatic test date expired.
Outfit incomplete — lamp, axe or lifeline missing.
Outfits stowed together instead of widely separated.
EEBDs with the indicator outside the green band or the seal broken.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — fire doors, dampers and closing appliances
what: Structural fire protection findings are dominated by doors held open and dampers that do not close.
detailBullets: Self-closing doors wedged, hooked or tied open.
Doors that do not latch, or with damaged seals and closers.
Dampers seized, or the indicator disagreeing with the blade.
Remote releases and ventilation stops inoperative or not proved at the fan.
Penetrations cut through divisions and not made good.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — detection and alarm systems
what: Detection findings usually come down to standing disablements and missing test records.
detailBullets: Zones or loops isolated and left isolated with no defect entry.
Detectors painted over, taped up or removed during works.
Monthly sample test not recorded; five-yearly full test overdue.
Standby batteries flat or beyond their service life.
No spare detector heads or test equipment on board.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — drills, muster and crew familiarity
what: Inspectors test the crew, not only the equipment; unfamiliarity is a common and serious finding.
evidence: Log book entry, signed, drill and training records
detailBullets: Crew unable to demonstrate donning an immersion suit or starting the emergency fire pump.
Muster list out of date after a crew change, or duties not understood.
Drill records generic, or drills not covering the required scenarios.
Fire party unable to locate and use an EEBD or a fireman's outfit.
Instructions and signage not in the working language of the crew.
Described generically as recurring themes. This app does not assert port State control deficiency codes — use the inspecting regime's own code list.

title: Recurring PSC themes — records and documentation
what: A great deal of equipment that is physically in order is written up as deficient because the record cannot be produced.
detailBullets: Service reports and certificates not on board, or filed where nobody can find them.
Checklists unsigned or not retained after the log entry is made.
Fire control plan superseded by a modification.
The maintenance plan not covering an installed system.
Export the register and the due list before arrival so the evidence is one file.

title: Preparing for the Safety Equipment survey
what: Everything falling due before the certificate expiry is listed, split by whether the ship can do it or a provider must, and planned against the port rotation.
detailBullets: Start from the certificate expiry and work backwards through the due list.
Separate ship's-staff tasks from provider tasks — the provider list drives the port planning.
Confirm provider approvals and flag acceptance before booking.
Reconcile the register against the Record of Equipment.
Close open deficiencies, or have the corrective action and target date documented.
Export the pack so the surveyor gets one file rather than a folder of paper.

title: Helicopter facilities: landing areas and winching areas
what: A ship fitted with a helicopter deck or a designated winching area must meet the construction, escape, drainage and fire-fighting requirements of SOLAS II-2/18.
evidence: Fire control plan, survey record, helideck certificate where applicable
detailBullets: A helicopter deck is a purpose-built landing area; a winching area is a clear area for hoisting only, with no landing.
The deck is of steel or other equivalent material; aluminium construction is subject to additional fire protection requirements.
Drainage is arranged so that spilled fuel runs off the deck and away from accommodation and other structures, and cannot enter the sea uncontrolled.
At least two access/escape routes are provided from the landing area.
The fire-fighting appliances of II-2/18.1.2 are stowed close to but clear of the area, ready for immediate use.
Signs, markings, perimeter safety net and tie-down points are maintained and clear of obstruction.
summaryTr: Helikopter güvertesi veya vinç (winching) alanı bulunan gemiler SOLAS II-2/18'in yapı, kaçış, drenaj ve yangınla mücadele gerekliliklerini karşılamalıdır.

title: Fire-fighting appliances at the helicopter deck
what: Foam, dry powder, CO2, at least two dual-purpose nozzles with hoses reaching any part of the deck, and the listed rescue equipment must be stowed near the landing area.
howOften: Weekly check; monthly inspection; annual service
byWhom: Ship's staff; foam sampled by a shore laboratory
evidence: Weekly and monthly checklists, foam analysis certificate, extinguisher service records
detailBullets: Foam application: the discharge rate and monitor or applicator arrangement follow the helideck's D-value as required by the regulation.
At least two dual-purpose nozzles and hoses able to reach any part of the helicopter deck.
Dry powder of at least 45 kg total, and CO2 of at least 18 kg total (or equivalent).
Rescue equipment kept ready: rescue axe, crowbar, bolt croppers, hook-type knife, heavy-duty hacksaw with spare blades, fire-resistant gloves and blanket, ladder, lifeline with harness.
Foam concentrate is sampled and analysed on the schedule required for fire-fighting foams; degraded concentrate is replaced, not topped up.
Appliances are stowed close enough to be immediately usable and far enough back to be reachable during a deck fire.
summaryTr: Helikopter güvertesinde köpük, kuru kimyevi toz, CO2, güverteye ulaşabilen iki adet çift amaçlı nozul ve belirtilen kurtarma teçhizatı hazır bulundurulur.

title: Preparing the ship before a helicopter arrives
what: The master and the helicopter pilot agree the operation in advance, and the deck is prepared and inspected before the aircraft is called in.
byWhom: Master, deck officer in charge, deck party
evidence: Pre-operation checklist, deck log entry, radio log
detailBullets: Agree in advance: type of operation (landing, winching, or vertical replenishment), time, ship's course and speed, and the radio frequency.
Pass the ship's heading, wind speed and relative direction, pitch and roll, and the state of the deck to the aircraft.
Clear the whole area of loose gear: caps, cardboard, rope tails, unsecured covers and rubbish become missiles in the downwash.
Aerials and any obstruction within the obstacle-free sector are lowered or struck as agreed.
The deck is dry and free of oil, grease and ice; wash down and dry it if there is any doubt.
Fire party is closed up and dressed, hoses run out and charged if required, and the deck is manned before the aircraft is called.
summaryTr: Kaptan ile pilot operasyonu önceden mutabık kalır; güverte hazırlanır ve helikopter çağrılmadan önce kontrol edilir.

title: Deck party, briefing and personal protective equipment
what: Everyone taking part is briefed, wears the correct protective equipment and knows the approach and escape routes before the aircraft arrives.
detailBullets: Everyone on the deck wears a helmet with chin strap, ear protection, eye protection, gloves, and a lifejacket where required.
Nothing is carried above shoulder height near a running rotor; approach and depart in the pilot's field of view.
Never approach a helicopter from the rear: the tail rotor is the hazard, and the aft sector is a no-go area.
Only approach when signalled by the aircrew, and only from the designated sector.
Passengers are briefed on seating, harnesses, life jackets and emergency exits before boarding.
Smoking is prohibited on and around the deck, and for the whole period the aircraft is on or near the ship.
summaryTr: Operasyona katılan herkes brifing alır, doğru koruyucu donanımı giyer ve helikopter gelmeden önce yaklaşma ve kaçış yollarını bilir.

title: Winching and hi-line transfers
what: In a winching transfer the aircraft does not land; the ship provides a clear area, a steady platform and a controlled hi-line.
byWhom: Deck officer in charge, deck party
detailBullets: The winching area is clear of obstructions with the marked clear zone maintained around it.
The hi-line is allowed to touch the deck or the sea before it is handled, so that accumulated static discharges.
The hi-line is never made fast to the ship, and is never taken round a fitting: it must be able to run free at any moment.
Slack is taken in hand over hand and kept clear of the deck; it is paid out if the aircraft rises or moves away.
Ship's course and speed are held steady, with the relative wind as agreed with the pilot.
The transfer is stopped immediately if the aircraft manoeuvres or the line fouls.
summaryTr: Vinçle transferde helikopter inmez; gemi açık bir alan, sabit bir platform ve kontrollü bir hi-line hattı sağlar. Hat asla gemiye bağlanmaz.

title: Helicopter refuelling and hangar facilities
what: Where a ship refuels or hangars helicopters, the fuel installation, its pumps, bonding and fire protection must meet SOLAS II-2/18.3.
howOften: Per operation; system tested to the maintenance plan
byWhom: Ship's staff; officer in charge of refuelling
evidence: Refuelling checklist, maintenance plan records, deck log entry
detailBullets: The fuel tank stowage is as far as practicable from accommodation, escape routes and embarkation stations.
Pumps have a remote stop from a safe position and a means of local shutdown, and the piping is capable of being isolated.
The aircraft and the refuelling equipment are electrically bonded before any connection is made.
Fire hoses are laid out and ready, and foam appliances are manned throughout the operation.
Refuelling with rotors running is only done where it is expressly permitted and under the agreed procedure.
Smoking, hot work and any naked light are prohibited in the area throughout.
summaryTr: Helikopter yakıt ikmali veya hangar tesisi bulunan gemilerde yakıt sistemi, pompalar, topraklama ve yangın korunması SOLAS II-2/18.3'e uygun olmalıdır.

title: Helicopter emergency: crash on deck
what: The response to an aircraft accident on or near the ship is planned, drilled and manned before every operation, not improvised.
evidence: Drill record, muster list, deck log entry
detailBullets: The fire party is closed up and equipped before the aircraft is called in, not summoned afterwards.
The immediate action is to protect the escape path of the occupants: apply foam to create and hold a clear route.
Rescue equipment stowed under II-2/18.1.2 is the kit used to break in — axe, crowbar, bolt croppers, hook knife, hacksaw.
The general alarm is sounded and the master informed; the ship manoeuvres as required for a person in the water.
A helicopter in the water beside the ship is treated as a man-overboard as well as a fire casualty.
The plan covers the aircraft on deck, alongside in the water, and a fire in the fuel installation.
sourceRef: SOLAS II-2/18; ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations
summaryTr: Gemide veya yakınında bir hava aracı kazasına müdahale önceden planlanır, tatbik edilir ve her operasyon öncesi ekip hazır bekletilir.

title: Ship/Shore Safety Check List
what: Before cargo, ballast, bunkering or tank cleaning starts alongside, the ship and the terminal complete the Ship/Shore Safety Check List together and agree the repetitive checks.
howOften: Before each transfer, with agreed repetitive checks during it
byWhom: Responsible officer and terminal representative, jointly
evidence: Signed Ship/Shore Safety Check List, declaration and repetitive check record
detailBullets: The list is completed jointly. A code letter against an item marks who verifies it and how it is to be re-checked.
Items marked for repetitive checking are re-verified at the agreed interval throughout the transfer, and the check is recorded.
Any item that cannot be answered yes is resolved before the operation starts; the operation does not begin on an open item.
Agreement covers the transfer plan, maximum rates, topping-off rates, and the emergency stop signal and procedure.
Means of communication and the language to be used are agreed, with a backup means identified.
The list does not replace the ship's or the terminal's own procedures; it is the record that both sides checked the same things.
sourceRef: ISGOTT (6th Edition), Ship/Shore Safety Check List
summaryTr: Yükleme, balast, yakıt ikmali veya tank temizliği başlamadan önce gemi ve terminal, Gemi/Sahil Emniyet Kontrol Listesini birlikte doldurur ve tekrarlı kontrolleri kararlaştırır.

title: Enclosed space entry on tankers
what: No one enters a cargo tank, pump room, cofferdam, duct keel or any other enclosed space without a valid permit, a tested atmosphere and a standby attendant.
howOften: Per entry; drill every two months (SOLAS III/19)
evidence: Entry permit, gas readings log, drill record
detailBullets: Test the atmosphere before entry and at the levels people will work at: oxygen 20.8%, hydrocarbon below 1% LFL, toxics below the occupational limit.
Test from outside the space; never enter to take the first reading.
Ventilation runs continuously before and throughout the entry, and the space is re-tested at intervals.
An attendant stays at the entrance with communications, and rescue equipment and a resuscitator are ready outside.
The permit is time-limited and is cancelled if conditions change, the ventilation stops, or the space is left unattended.
Hydrogen sulphide, benzene and oxygen deficiency from inert gas or rust are all invisible: only the meter says the space is safe.
sourceRef: ISGOTT (6th Edition); SOLAS III/19; IMO Res. A.1050(27)
summaryTr: Kargo tankı, pompa dairesi, koferdam veya kapalı mahalle geçerli izin, ölçülmüş atmosfer ve dışarıda bekleyen gözcü olmadan girilmez.

title: Hot work on a tanker
what: Hot work outside a designated workshop requires a permit, a gas-free certificate where applicable, a fire watch and the master's authorisation.
byWhom: Master authorises; officer in charge supervises
evidence: Hot work permit, gas readings, fire watch record
detailBullets: Hot work is planned so that it is done in a designated space wherever possible; work outside one is the exception, not the routine.
The space and all adjacent spaces, including those below and above and on the other side of a bulkhead, are tested and certified safe.
Readings are repeated before work restarts after any break and at the intervals set in the permit.
A dedicated fire watch is posted with extinguishing means, and remains after the work stops for the period set in the permit.
Cargo, ballast and tank cleaning operations are suspended where the permit requires it.
The permit names the exact location, the work, the period and the person in charge; it is not a standing authority.
summaryTr: Atölye dışındaki sıcak işler için izin, gerekli hallerde gazdan arındırma sertifikası, yangın gözcüsü ve kaptanın yetkilendirmesi gerekir.

title: Static electricity and loading precautions
what: Static-accumulator oils and water-mist conditions can generate an incendive discharge, so initial loading rates, dipping and sampling are controlled.
evidence: Cargo plan, deck log entry, tank atmosphere record
detailBullets: Load at a reduced initial rate until the tank inlet is well submerged and turbulence has settled.
Do not dip, sample or ullage a static-accumulator cargo through a non-inerted tank for the settling time required after loading stops.
Metallic equipment lowered into a tank is earthed to the ship's structure before it goes in, and stays earthed throughout.
Free-fall of cargo into a tank, and water or steam jetting into a non-inerted tank, are avoided.
An inerted tank held below the flammable range removes the hazard; this is why inert gas is kept on and the tank is kept below 8% oxygen.
Synthetic ropes, plastic buckets and unearthed tank cleaning machines are all recognised static sources.
summaryTr: Statik biriktirici kargolarda ve su-sis koşullarında kıvılcım oluşabilir; bu yüzden ilk yükleme hızı, iskandil ve numune alma kontrol altındadır.

title: Keeping cargo tanks inerted
what: Cargo tanks on an inerted ship are kept at positive pressure with an oxygen content at or below 8% by volume, and the system is checked before and during every operation.
howOften: Continuous; checked before and during each cargo operation
evidence: Inert gas log, oxygen analyser calibration record, deck log
detailBullets: Oxygen content at or below 8% by volume, and the tanks kept at a positive pressure at all times.
The oxygen analyser is calibrated on the schedule required and before critical operations; an uncalibrated reading is not evidence.
The deck water seal and the non-return arrangement are checked: they are what stops cargo gas backing into the machinery space.
Discharging, deballasting and tank cleaning of inerted tanks are only done with the system running and in specification.
Alarms and trips — high oxygen, low pressure, high gas temperature, low water level in the seal — are tested at the required intervals.
Purging before gas freeing is done so that the tank passes out of, not through, the flammable range.
summaryTr: İnert sistemli gemilerde kargo tankları pozitif basınçta ve oksijen hacimce %8 veya altında tutulur; sistem her operasyon öncesi ve sırasında kontrol edilir.

title: Portable gas detection: the right instrument, calibrated
what: Each hazard needs the instrument that measures it, calibrated and bump-tested, and readings are recorded rather than remembered.
howOften: Before each use; calibrated to the maker's schedule
evidence: Calibration certificates, bump-test log, gas readings record
detailBullets: A catalytic (LFL) meter does not work in an inert atmosphere: use a tankscope or an equivalent instrument for oxygen-deficient tanks.
Oxygen, hydrocarbon, hydrogen sulphide and benzene each need their own measurement; one reading is not a clearance for the space.
Bump-test before use and calibrate on the maker's schedule; record both.
Take readings at several levels, and remember that heavier-than-air vapours collect low down.
Personal H2S monitors are worn where the cargo or the terminal requires them, and their alarms are not silenced.
Sample lines and probes are checked for length, condition and blockage before they are trusted.
summaryTr: Her tehlike için doğru cihaz gerekir: kalibre edilmiş, bump-test yapılmış ve okumaları kayda geçirilmiş olmalıdır.

title: Moorings and emergency towing-off pennants alongside
what: The ship stays moored so that it can be moved or let go quickly, with emergency towing-off pennants rigged where the terminal requires them.
evidence: Mooring plan, deck log, watch handover record
detailBullets: Moorings are tended so that the ship stays within the manifold's working range as it changes draught.
Emergency towing-off pennants, where required, are rigged fore and aft, outboard, with the eye near the water and secured to bitts.
A means of escape from the ship to the shore is maintained at all times, safely rigged, lit and with a lifebuoy and line beside it.
The engine, steering and crew readiness for departure are as agreed with the terminal.
A continuous deck watch is kept: the whole point of the checklist items is that someone is there to see them change.
Fire wires and moorings are checked at every watch handover and after any significant change of draught or weather.
summaryTr: Gemi hızla hareket ettirilebilecek veya bırakılabilecek şekilde bağlı tutulur; terminalin istediği yerlerde acil çekme halatları donatılır.

title: Carriage of the IAMSAR Manual Volume III
what: Every ship must carry an up-to-date copy of Volume III of the IAMSAR Manual, the volume written for mobile facilities.
howOften: Carried at all times; kept up to date
detailBullets: Volume III — Mobile Facilities — is the volume carried on board; Volumes I and II are for SAR organisations and mission co-ordination.
It is the ship's reference for acting as a first responder, an on-scene co-ordinator, or a facility taking part in a search.
Amendments are entered so that the copy on board matches the current edition.
It is kept where the bridge team can reach it immediately, not filed away with the ship's library.
It complements, and does not replace, the ship's own SOLAS III/19 muster list and emergency procedures.
Familiarity with the search patterns and the initial actions belongs to bridge team training, not to the moment of the distress.
sourceRef: SOLAS V/21.2; IAMSAR Manual Volume III
summaryTr: Her gemi, mobil tesisler için yazılmış olan IAMSAR El Kitabı Cilt III'ün güncel bir nüshasını taşımak zorundadır.

title: Initial actions on receiving a distress message
what: Acknowledge, establish the position and the nature of the distress, proceed if able, and report — in that order, and without waiting for instructions.
evidence: Radio log, deck log, GMDSS log
detailBullets: Acknowledge receipt, and relay the message if there is any doubt that a rescue co-ordination centre has it.
Record everything: time received, position, nature of distress, number of persons, and the identity of the casualty.
Plot the casualty's position and your own, work out the course and the time to reach it, and inform the RCC.
Proceed at best speed unless it would put your own ship in danger; if you cannot, say so and say why.
Prepare the ship on the way: lookouts posted, rescue boat and recovery equipment ready, medical and accommodation prepared.
Keep a continuous listening watch on the distress frequency and log every transmission.
summaryTr: Tehlike mesajı alındığında sırasıyla: teyit et, mevkii ve tehlikenin niteliğini belirle, mümkünse yola çık ve rapor et.

title: Man overboard: the recovery turns
what: The turn used depends on when the loss was noticed, and the choice is made before it is needed, not worked out at the moment.
detailBullets: Immediate action: hard over towards the side the person went over, release a lifebuoy with light and smoke, sound the alarm, post a lookout, mark the position.
Williamson turn — for a person missed some time ago and for reduced visibility: it returns the ship onto its reciprocal track.
Anderson (single) turn — fastest, for an immediate sighting, on a ship that manoeuvres well; it does not regain the original track.
Scharnov turn — returns the ship onto its track astern of the original position; only usable when the loss occurred some time ago.
Rescue boat, recovery equipment and a first-aid party are readied while the turn is being made.
The lookout does not leave the person: keeping the sighting is worth more than any manoeuvre.
summaryTr: Kullanılacak dönüş, kaybın ne zaman fark edildiğine bağlıdır; seçim o an değil, önceden yapılır.

title: Search patterns for a single ship
what: A search is run to a pattern agreed with the co-ordinator, with a chosen track spacing, so that the area is covered and the coverage can be reported.
evidence: Search plan, deck log, report to the RCC
detailBullets: Expanding square (SS): for a small search area and a well-known datum — legs increase by the track spacing, starting at the datum.
Sector search (VS): for a small area with a good datum, repeatedly crossing it from different directions; good for a person in the water.
Parallel track (PS): for a large area with an uncertain position, run as parallel legs at the chosen track spacing.
Track line search (TS): along the casualty's intended track, outbound and return, when the ship is proceeding to the scene.
Track spacing is chosen for the target size, the visibility and the sea state, and is reported with the coverage achieved.
Datum is moved for drift — leeway and current — before and during the search, and the search is re-planned as it moves.
summaryTr: Arama, koordinatörle mutabık kalınan bir paterne ve seçilen bir hat aralığına göre yürütülür; böylece alan taranır ve kapsama raporlanabilir.

title: Acting as On-Scene Co-ordinator
what: The first suitable facility on scene co-ordinates the search until an RCC appoints someone, and hands over cleanly when relieved.
evidence: OSC log, situation reports to the RCC
detailBullets: Take the role if you are first on scene and no one has been appointed; tell the RCC that you have.
Co-ordinate the search: allocate areas and patterns, set safe separation and communication frequencies, and avoid collision risk between facilities.
Keep a plot of what has been searched and by whom, so that the coverage is a fact and not an impression.
Send situation reports to the RCC: what has been searched, what was found, what the weather is, and what you need.
Co-ordinate on-scene safety, including for aircraft operating low over the search area.
Hand over to the relieving facility with the plot, the coverage and the plan, and record the time of handover.
summaryTr: Olay yerine ilk ulaşan uygun tesis, bir kurtarma koordinasyon merkezi atama yapana kadar aramayı koordine eder ve devrederken temiz bir devir yapar.

title: Recovering persons from the water
what: Every ship must have a plan and the means to recover persons from the water, and the equipment is prepared before it is needed.
evidence: Recovery plan, drill record, deck log
detailBullets: SOLAS III/17-1 requires ship-specific plans and procedures for recovery, taking account of the ship's freeboard and the equipment carried.
The plan names the equipment, the people, and the method for a conscious survivor, an unconscious one, and several at once.
A survivor recovered from cold water is kept horizontal: lifting vertically can cause circulatory collapse.
Rescue boat, recovery ladder, nets, slings, lighting and communications are prepared during the approach, not after arriving.
Survivors are counted, identified, warmed and given medical attention, and their details reported to the co-ordinator.
Recovery over the lee side, with the ship providing a lee, is normally safer than the weather side.
sourceRef: SOLAS III/17-1; MSC.1/Circ.1447; IAMSAR Manual Volume III
summaryTr: Her gemide, denizden insan kurtarmak için bir plan ve gerekli araçlar bulunmalı ve teçhizat ihtiyaç duyulmadan önce hazırlanmalıdır.

title: Distress communications and homing on the casualty
what: Distress alerting, on-scene communications and homing all use the GMDSS equipment the ship already carries, and the watch is continuous.
howOften: Continuous watch; equipment tested to schedule
evidence: GMDSS log, radio log, equipment test records
detailBullets: MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger; PAN PAN for urgency; a DSC distress alert is acknowledged and followed by voice on the working frequency.
A relayed distress (MAYDAY RELAY) is sent when there is doubt that anyone else has heard the casualty.
SART and AIS-SART respond to a 9 GHz radar and appear on the display as a line of blips towards the target; identify the pattern before believing the range.
406 MHz EPIRB alerts reach the RCC via satellite; homing on scene uses the 121.5 MHz beacon and the SART.
On-scene traffic uses the frequency the co-ordinator sets, and everything is logged with times.
Equipment tests — daily, weekly and monthly as required by SOLAS IV — are what makes the equipment work on the day.
sourceRef: IAMSAR Manual Volume III; SOLAS IV
summaryTr: Tehlike ihbarı, olay yeri haberleşmesi ve yön bulma, geminin taşıdığı GMDSS teçhizatı ile yapılır ve dinleme nöbeti kesintisizdir.
